title: Dermatology & MedSpa Office Scope Tasks: Janitorial Checklist and Labor Hours
seoTitle: Dermatology MedSpa Office Scope Tasks: Janitorial Checklist & Hours
metaDescription: Dermatology medspa office scope tasks by daily, weekly, and monthly tier, with 1.6–2.5 labor hours per night for 3,200 sq ft. Price it in our calculator.
excerpt: A dermatology or medspa janitorial scope has to separate clinical turnover from nightly cleaning and account for treatment rooms that run slower than open office space. This checklist lists every task by frequency and shows which ones add labor hours to your bid.
quickAnswer: A complete dermatology and medspa scope covers nightly treatment-room floor disinfection, restroom sanitation, high-touch point disinfection, and lobby and retail glass, plus weekly high dusting and monthly floor machine work. A 3,200 sq ft suite with three restrooms typically needs about 1.6 to 2.5 labor hours per night, versus roughly 1 hour for the same area of open office. Specialty tasks such as dwell-time disinfection, laser-room dusting, and grout scrubbing are what push the hours above standard office rates.

blocks.text: Start With the Division of Labor Between Clinic Staff and the Crew

The most common scope dispute in dermatology and medspa contracts is not about price. It is about who wipes what. Clinical staff clean and disinfect treatment tables, procedure trays, device handpieces, and countertops between patients, and they manage sharps and regulated medical waste. The janitorial crew handles the nightly reset: floors, restrooms, waste, sinks, walls, doors, and every high-touch point that staff do not reach during a packed clinic day. When this division is not written into the scope, the crew skips the procedure room because they assume staff covered it, and staff assume the crew did a full terminal clean.

Write the scope so each room type has its own task list, its own frequency, and a note about which surfaces are off-limits. Laser handpieces, cryotherapy units, microneedling devices, and anything plugged into a medical-grade outlet should be excluded from janitorial contact entirely. Crews dust the device housing exterior and the cart only if your practice manager approves it in writing.

blocks.caption: Nightly scope of work for a dermatology and medspa suite
rows: Empty non-regulated trash, disinfect sink, faucet, door handles, light switches, stool seats and bases, exterior of cabinets; dust mop and damp mop floor
Hospital-grade quat at label dwell; microfiber flat mop
Same as exam plus floor disinfection to wall base and under table, wipe exterior of exam light arm
Disinfect toilets, urinals, sinks, grab bars, changing bench; refill paper and soap; mop with disinfectant
Disinfect check-in counter, pens, card terminal surround, chair arms; vacuum entry mat; dust mop and damp mop
Remove fingerprints from glass shelving, entry doors, and partitions
Clean counters, sink, microwave inside and out, fridge handles; empty trash
Empty trash and recycling, dust mop and damp mop or vacuum, spot-clean walls at cart height

blocks.text: Those minutes add up to roughly 117 to 166 minutes, or about 2 to 2.75 labor hours for a single crew member. Experienced two-person crews compress that to about 1.6 to 2.5 total labor hours because one person runs restrooms and wet work while the other handles trash, dusting, and dry floor work. Compare that with the ISSA production benchmark of about 3,500 sq ft per hour for a general office, which would clean the same 3,200 sq ft in under an hour plus restroom time.

blocks.title: Spray-and-wipe is not disinfection
blocks.text: If a bidder's labor estimate assumes 90 minutes for this suite, they are probably skipping dwell time. EPA-registered disinfectants must stay visibly wet for the label contact time, often 3 to 10 minutes, to achieve the claims on the label. Ask each vendor which product they use and what dwell time their crews follow.

Weekly and monthly items are where scopes get thin. Many vendor templates for generic offices list high dusting quarterly, but laser and IPL rooms generate fine particulate that settles on vents, light fixtures, and device carts. In a dermatology suite, these belong on a weekly cadence.

items: Weekly: high dust supply and return vents, light lenses, door frames, and tops of cabinets in laser and procedure rooms.
Weekly: detail-clean baseboards and wall bases in treatment rooms where cart wheels and stools leave marks.
Weekly: scrub restroom grout lines and floor drains with a deck brush; tile floors need it more than LVT.
Weekly: polish stainless kick plates, retail fixtures, and elevator lobby surfaces if your suite owns them.
Monthly: machine scrub or burnish LVT corridors and reception; spot extract any carpeted offices.
Monthly: wash waste receptacles inside and out, and wipe interior of breakroom refrigerator if staff approve.
Quarterly: full scrub-and-recoat or deep restorative clean of hard floors, amortized at $0.03 to $0.06 per sq ft per month.

blocks.text: Specialty Tasks That Push Labor Above Standard Office Rates

Each of the tasks below adds measurable time compared with a general office scope. When you compare bids, look for vendors who name these tasks explicitly. A bid that reads like a generic office checklist is cheaper because it omits them, not because the vendor is more efficient.

blocks.caption: Specialty tasks and their labor impact
rows: Dwell-time disinfection of floors and touch points
Surfaces must stay wet for label contact time; crews must sequence rooms to allow dwell
Separate pads, cloths, and buckets for restrooms vs treatment rooms vs lobby
Hard-floor damp mopping in every treatment room
Cannot be skipped like carpet vacuuming on light nights
Benches, hooks, mirrors, and higher soil from changing
Fingerprints on every visit; needs streak-free finish
Ladder work around devices and ceiling vents

blocks.text: Converting Labor Hours Into a Monthly Price

Once you have hours, you can sanity-check any bid. Standard janitorial labor bills at $35 to $65 per hour and specialty or medical-trained labor at $55 to $95 per hour. At 2 labor hours per night and $55 per hour, a nightly visit costs about $110 in labor; vendors add supervision, supplies, insurance, and margin, landing near $300 to $540 per visit for a 3,200 sq ft suite with three restrooms. Multiply by 21.65 visits per month for five nights a week, using 4.33 weeks per month, and you reach roughly $6,800 to $11,700 per month. Three nights a week at 13 visits brings that to about $4,300 to $7,300.

items.name: List rooms and counts
items.text: Count treatment rooms, procedure rooms, restrooms, and retail fixtures. Measure cleanable square footage, not rentable.

items.name: Assign minutes per room
items.text: Use the nightly table above as a baseline and adjust for tile versus LVT and number of changing areas.

items.name: Add weekly and monthly tasks as amortized minutes
items.text: A 60-minute weekly high-dust task adds about 12 minutes to each of five nightly visits.

items.name: Multiply by a realistic hourly rate
items.text: Use $55 to $95 per hour for crews trained in bloodborne pathogens and dwell-time disinfection.

items.name: Compare to each bid
items.text: A bid well below your labor math is cutting tasks; a bid far above it should justify extra services in writing.

blocks.text: Tools That Keep the Scope Efficient

Tool choice directly affects the minutes in your scope. An Unger 15-gallon dual-bucket SmartColor system keeps clean solution separated from dirty rinse water, so the crew is not redepositing soil from one treatment room into the next, and its red and blue compartments support the color-coding your scope should require. For treatment rooms, a Rubbermaid HYGEN 18-inch microfiber flat mop with an onboard reservoir lets crews switch to a fresh pad per room with no bucket at all, which is faster and prevents cross-contamination. For glass retail shelving and entry doors, an Ettore Master Brass 14-inch squeegee with replaceable rubber gives a streak-free finish in fewer passes than cloth alone.

blocks.title: Document training in the scope
blocks.text: Require that every crew member assigned to the suite has completed OSHA bloodborne pathogens training within the last 12 months and has been offered hepatitis B vaccination. Add a line that the vendor must keep Safety Data Sheets for every chemical on site under HazCom.

faqs.q: How many labor hours does a medspa need per night?
faqs.a: A 3,200 sq ft suite with eight treatment rooms and three restrooms usually takes 1.6 to 2.5 labor hours per night when crews follow disinfectant dwell times and damp mop every hard floor. A 1,800 sq ft studio typically needs 1 to 1.5 hours. Generic office production rates of 3,500 sq ft per hour understate the time.

faqs.q: Should janitorial crews clean treatment tables and devices?
faqs.a: Crews should not touch medical devices, laser handpieces, or anything on a procedure tray. Treatment table vinyl is normally disinfected by clinical staff between patients; some practices add a nightly wipe-down by the crew as a second layer. Put the decision in writing so both sides know who owns each surface.

faqs.q: What tasks are usually excluded from a dermatology cleaning scope?
faqs.a: Regulated medical waste, sharps containers, biohazard spills involving significant blood, medical equipment, window exteriors, and carpet hot-water extraction are commonly excluded or priced separately. Spill response for blood should follow your exposure control plan, and vendors should only perform it if their staff are trained and equipped.

faqs.q: How often should hard floors in a medspa be machine scrubbed?
faqs.a: Corridors and reception typically need monthly machine scrubbing or burnishing, with a quarterly deep scrub or recoat. Treatment rooms with LVT usually need only nightly damp mopping and quarterly restorative work. Budget $0.03 to $0.06 per sq ft per month for an amortized floor program.

faqs.q: Can we use a day porter instead of nightly cleaning?
faqs.a: A day porter is useful in busy clinics for restroom checks, reception touch points, and spill response during patient hours, but it does not replace a full nightly clean. Many larger dermatology groups pair a 4-hour midday porter with nightly service.
